title: The Monkey and the Cat
text:
Bertrand the monkey and Raton the cat lived in the same house and shared the same master. They were a pair of rascals, and nothing in the house was safe from them.

One day they found some chestnuts roasting in the fireplace. Bertrand wanted them badly, but he had no intention of burning his own fingers. So he turned to the cat with his best flattery. Brother, he said, this is the day to show your talent. With paws as quick as yours, you could have those chestnuts out in no time. If I had your gifts, they would already be ours.

Raton was flattered. He reached into the ashes carefully, drew back his paw, reached in again, and flicked out one chestnut, then another, then a third. Each time he did, Bertrand gobbled the chestnut up.

Then a servant girl came in, and the two thieves ran off. Raton, La Fontaine says, was not very pleased. He had burned his paws, and Bertrand had eaten every chestnut.
lesson: Be wary of a partner who praises your skill just when there is a risky job to do. Check who takes the burns and who eats the chestnuts.
people: Bertrand the monkey, Raton the cat
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book IX, The Monkey and the Cat (Le Singe et le Chat), 1679
